title: DSGym: A Standardized and Holistic Framework for Evaluating and Training Data Science Agents
one_liner: DSGym evaluates data-science agents inside real execution environments so they must use the data, run analyses, and justify conclusions with actual evidence.
lead: A data-science agent should do more than talk about an analysis. It should load the dataset, choose a method, run code, inspect the results, and report findings that the data actually supports. DSGym is built around that full loop, because many older benchmarks can be solved by writing plausible text without touching the data at all.

problem.h2: Why current data-science benchmarks can mislead
paras: Many existing benchmarks use different interfaces, different scoring rules, and tasks that are too narrow to compare cleanly. Worse, some tasks can be solved without real data use. An agent can produce a convincing answer from prior knowledge or benchmark shortcuts, which means the benchmark rewards style and recall instead of actual analysis.

This is especially harmful in science settings because the whole point of a data-science agent is evidence-based work. If the benchmark does not force the agent to inspect the dataset, run code, and validate a claim, then a high score does not mean the agent can do the job.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Put data-science tasks into a shared execution framework with quality filtering, data-grounded task design, and execution-verified training data so that agents must earn answers from the dataset itself.

mechanism.h2: Why this works: standardize the environment and block shortcut answers
paras: DSGym provides a modular execution environment where tasks, tools, and agent scaffolds follow the same structure. That standardization helps because scores from different tasks become comparable, and new tasks can be added without inventing a fresh benchmark interface each time.

The framework also filters and extends the task set. DSGym-Tasks cleans up existing benchmarks by removing weak tasks and shortcut-solvable examples. DSBio adds expert-written bioinformatics work, and DSPredict adds hard prediction problems from several scientific areas. The training side uses execution-verified synthesis, which matters because generated examples count only when code actually runs and produces the intended evidence.

stages.s: Dataset, task prompt, and execution environment
Agent must inspect data and run analysis code
Framework checks outputs against task-specific rules
Comparable evaluation plus trainable analysis traces

math.words: A task counts as solved only if the agent completes the requested analysis and its result is supported by executable evidence from the dataset. The main quantity is the fraction of tasks that pass those grounded checks.
symbols: tasks where the agent's code runs and the produced result passes the benchmark's evidence checks
all evaluated tasks in the suite
share of tasks solved with data-backed evidence rather than unsupported text

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: It writes plausible answers for 16 tasks, but only 11 of those include code that runs and produces the checked result.
The gap between 16 plausible answers and 11 verified answers is the point of DSGym: a benchmark should reward the verified set, because only those answers are actually supported by the data.

math.note: The paper's central criticism is that many benchmark tasks can be answered without using the data. Grounded success is the compact quantity that removes that shortcut.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Create three tasks over a small scientific dataset: summarize a relationship, fit a prediction model, and validate a claim against held-out data. Run one evaluation that scores final text only and another that requires code execution plus evidence checks. Then compare the same agent under both settings.
The demo should show that text-only scoring overestimates ability because some fluent answers collapse once the framework demands code, data use, and checked outputs.
demo.metric_eq: shortcut_gap = text_only_score - grounded_success ; verified_yield = accepted_training_examples / generated_training_examples
demo.closing: A useful data-science benchmark should certify that the agent used the data and produced evidence, because that is the work users actually need.

items.b: Verification may miss subtle scientific errors.
items.html: Passing code checks does not guarantee correct scientific reasoning, because an agent can run the wrong analysis cleanly if the task's validator is too shallow.
A shared framework improves comparison, but it may discourage unusual workflows if the tool interface does not expose them, because agents can only use what the environment makes available.

items.b: Synthetic training traces can bias behavior.
items.html: Execution-verified synthesis improves reliability, but the agent may inherit the synthesis pipeline's preferred analysis style if the generated examples are too uniform because repeated traces can push the model toward one narrow workflow.

The paper extends beyond cleaned-up legacy tasks by adding expert and prediction-heavy suites, because broad coverage is necessary if the benchmark is meant to stand in for real scientific analysis work.

charts.title: Older fragmented benchmark setup
charts.note: Legacy setups mix interfaces and leave shortcut-solvable tasks in place, so a high score may not reflect real analysis ability.

charts.title: DSGym framework
charts.note: The paper's case study shows that a 2,000-example verified training set improves a 4B model because the framework can both evaluate and generate grounded training traces.
